mcqs.question: Anteflexion of the uterus is at the level of ___.
mcqs.explanation: Anteflexion of the uterus is seen at the level of the internal os. (Mnemonic - V for version, V for vagina ) The uterus normally lies in a position of anteversion and anteflexion . mcqs.subject: OBGYN
mcqs.question: A G3P2L2 woman presents in her third trimester with vaginal leaking. On PV examination, the anterior lip of the cervix can be palpated . What is the position of her uterus and the ligament that maintains this position?
mcqs.explanation: In the given clinical scenario, the uterus is anteverted as the anterior lip of the cervix was palpable . The round ligament helps maintain the anteversion of the uterus during pregnancy. However, the anteversion in the non-pregnant uterus is maintained by both the uterosacral ligament and round ligament . (Mnemonic - V for version, V for vagina ) The uterus normally lies in a position of anteversion and anteflexion . In the anteverted position, the external os is directed downward and backwards. On vaginal examination , the fingers come in contact with the anterior lip of the cervix as it is the lowest part. When the uterus is retroverted, the cervix is directed downward and forwards. The lowest part of the cervix becomes either the external os or its posterior lip. Anteflexion is seen at the level of the internal os.Angle of anteversion Angle of anteflexion Angle between thecervix and vagina Angle betweencervix and uter us 90o 120o20

mcqs.subject: OBGYN
mcqs.question: A multiparous woman presented with a urethrocele , due to weakness of the urogenital diaphragm. What is this structure also known as?
mcqs.explanation: The urogenital diaphragm is also known as the triangular ligament . The urogenital diaphragm extends from the pubic arch anteriorly to the central point of the perineum posteriorly and consists of two layers of fascia through which pass the vagina and the urethra. The central point of the female perineum lies between the vagina and the rectum. Urogenital triangle: • Present between 2 ischiopubic rami • Stretching transversely across the rami there are 3 membranes. • From above downwards the membranes are as follows : • Superior fascia of urogenital diaphragm • Inferior fascia of urogenital diaphragm • Membranous layer of superficial perineal fascia21

mcqs.subject: OBGYN
mcqs.question: What is the cavity of the uterus lined by?

options.a: Single layer of ciliated columnar epithelium
options.b: Double layer of ciliated columnar epithelium
options.c: Single layer of ciliated cuboidal epithelium
options.d: Double layer of ciliated cuboidal epithelium

mcqs.explanation: The uterine cavity is lined by a single layer of ciliated columnar epithelium . The wall of the uterus consists of 3 layers: • Perimetrium is the serous coat adherent to the underlying muscle . • Myometrium - it consists of thick bundles of muscles that form 3 distinct layers during pregnancy: • Outer longitudinal • Inner circular • Middle interlacing called living ligature • Endometrium - It is the mucous lining of the cavity. It consists of lamina propria and surface epithelium which is a single layer of ciliated columnar epithelium .

mcqs.subject: OBGYN
mcqs.question: A woman with regular menstrual cycles is undergoing an ultrasound on the 14th day of her cycle . What will the endometrial thickness be?
mcqs.explanation: During ovulation, the thickness of the endometrium is around 11 mm.Phase Endometrial thickne ss Immediately after menstruati on 1-2 mm Early proliferative phase 5-7 mm Secretory phase 7-16 mm22 Phase Endometrial thickne ss Preovulatory phase up to11 mm Postmenopausal <4 mm Postmenopausal - abnormal , requires biopsy >4 mm

mcqs.subject: OBGYN
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding uterine anatomy?

options.a: Round ligaments receive their blood supply from Sampson's artery
options.b: Transverse cervical ligaments are also called cardinal ligaments
options.c: Uterine innervation is by the pudendal nerve plexus
options.d: Lymphatic drainage is primarily to the obturator, internal and external iliac nodes .

mcqs.explanation: The uterus is innervated by the fibers of the uterovaginal plexus , also known as the Frankenhauser ganglion. Option A: Round ligaments receive their blood supply from Sampson's artery which represents the anastomosis of the uterine artery and ovarian artery. Option B: The cardinal ligaments are also called transverse cervical ligaments or Mackenrodt ligaments . They consist primarily of perivascular connective tissue . They attach to the posterolateral pelvic walls near the origin of the internal iliac artery and surround the vessels supplying the uterus and vagina . Option D: Lymphatic drainage of the uterus is primarily to the obturator and internal and external iliac nodes . One theory of endometriosis, states lymphatic spread as cause for seeding in the pelvis.

mcqs.subject: OBGYN
mcqs.question: A gynecologist is performing a hysterectomy . She accidentally nicks the ureter in the ureteric canal as it pierces the Mackenrodt's ligaments . Which vessels are likely to be damaged here?

options.a: Uterine artery above and the uterine plexus of veins below
options.b: Uterine plexus of veins above and the uterine artery below
options.c: Ovarian artery above and the uterine artery below
options.d: Uterine artery above and the ovarian artery below

mcqs.explanation: The uterine artery above and uterine venous plexus below are likely to be damaged here, as the ureter is present between these vessels . The ureter pierces the Mackenrodt's ligament , forming the ureteric canal. In this canal, the ureter is crossed by the uterine artery above and the uterine plexus of veins below , thus being present in between the uterine vessels . The ureteric canal provides the necessary room for normal peristalsis , without pressure from the surrounding structures . After leaving the ureteric canal, the ureter passes forwards and medially to reach the bladder . It is 1-2 cm away from the cervix.23

mcqs.subject: OBGYN
mcqs.question: You take a culture swab from the portio vaginalis of a woman having foul smelling vaginal discharge. What is this region also known as?
mcqs.explanation: Portio vaginalis or exocervix is the other name for the vaginal part of the cervix. Cervix is the lowermost part of the uterus extending from the histological internal os to the external os. It is cylindrical in shape measuring 2.5 cm in length and diameter . Cervix is made up of 10 % muscle and the rest is collagen , elastin , and proteoglycan . The lining of the cervix has the following parts: • Exocervix - also known as portio vaginalis. It is lined by non keratinized stratified squamous epithelium . • Endocervix - it is lined by high columnar, ciliated epithelium . • Endocervical glands - secrete alkaline mucus. When enlarged , they form swellings called Nabothian follicles /cysts . • Transformation zone - the epithelium gradually changes from columnar to squamous in this region.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: The newborn eye is usually ______.
mcqs.explanation: A newborn is usually hypermetropic by +2D to +3D. The anteroposterior (AP) diameter of the eyeball at birth is about 16.5 mm, which is about 70% of the adult size. This reduced axial length causes light to converge behind the retina, leading to12 hypermetropia . Additionally , the corneal diameter at birth is 10 mm. The adult size (11.7 mm) is attained by 2 years of age . The orbit is more divergent (50\260) as compared to adult (45\260). Note : The lacrimal glands are underdeveloped in a newborn and, hence , do not secrete tears.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: At what age would a child attain full visual acuity ?
mcqs.explanation: Full visual acuity is attained by the age of 6 years. Important milestones in visual development are: • At birth, there is no central fixation, and the eyes move randomly. • By the first month of life , the fixation reflex starts developing and becomes established by 6 months. • By 3 months, binocular vision is established . • By 6 months, macular stereopsis and accommodation reflex are fully developed . • By 6 years of age , full visual acuity (6/6) is attained .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old lady presents with the abnormality as shown below . She is diagnosed with uveal melanoma. What is the embryological origin of the cells involved?
mcqs.explanation: Uveal melanomas arise from uveal melanocytes . Uveal and conjunctival melanocytes are derived from the neural crest cells .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding the development of the eye ?

options.a: The macula is fully developed at birth.
options.c: The cornea attains normal diameter by 2 years.
options.d: Full visual acuity is attained by 6 years of age .

mcqs.explanation: The macula is fully developed by 4–6 months of age . Apart from the macula, the rest of the retina is fully developed at birth. Postnatal Development of Eye : • 3 Months - Binocular single vision develops . • 4-6 Months - Macula fully develops . Fusional reflexes , stereopsis , and accommodation become well developed • 6 Months - Fixation, which had started developing in the first month is now complete • 2 Years - Cornea develops to the normal adult diameter • 6 Years - Visual acuity fully develops and reaches 6/6 • The lens, however, continues to grow throughout the life13

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: By how many weeks of embryonic development does the optic groove appear?
mcqs.explanation: The optic groove appears by 3 weeks . By approximately day 22 , 2 small grooves appear on either side of the developing forebrain in the neural folds , these are called optic grooves. As the neural tube closes , these grooves develop outpouchings called optic vesicles . These optic vesicles extend from the forebrain to the surface ectoderm .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Embryonic development of ciliary muscles is from _______.
mcqs.explanation: Embryonic development of ciliary muscles is from the neural crest.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: After conception , the canal of Schlemm appears by __________________ .
mcqs.explanation: 14 The canal of Schlemm appears by the 4th month after conception .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: What is the anteroposterior diameter of the adult eyeball ?
mcqs.explanation: The anteroposterior (AP) diameter of the adult eye is 24 mm/2.4 cm. At birth, the average axial length of the eyeball is 16.5 mm. By 3 years, it grows rapidly to approximately 23 mm. From 3 to 14 years of age , the axial length gradually increases by a further 1 mm, bringing it to the adult size of 24 mm. This overall adjustment in the eye size, including the refractive power , is called emmetropization.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 34-year-old lady comes to the clinic complaining of problems in her vision. On perimetry , a visual field defect as shown below is obtained . Which of the following vessels does not supply the anatomical location of the lesion?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows bitemporal hemianopia, a defect caused by optic chiasmal lesions . The middle cerebral artery does not supply the optic chiasma. Blood supply of optic chiasma: • Anterior cerebral artery - dorsal chiasma • Anterior communicating artery - ventral chiasma • Internal carotid artery - ventral chiasma • Superior hypophyseal artery - ventral (branch of internal carotid artery).

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A college student comes to the OPD for refractive error testing . Her eyes are dilated using tropicamide. Which of the following statements is false about the structure this drug acts on?

options.a: It is triangular in cross section .
options.b: There are around 30-40 processes in pars plana and pars plicata
options.c: Its epithelium is derived from the anterior edge of the optic cup .
options.d: The pars plana is approximately 4.5 mm from the limbus.

mcqs.explanation: Tropicamide is a cycloplegic drug that acts on the ciliary body to cause mydriasis for refractory error testing . The ciliary body is a triangular structure that contains 60-70 ciliary processes in15 each eye , present on the pars plicata. The pars plana is 4.5mm from the limbus while the distance between the equator and the limbus is 14mm . The ciliary epithelium is derived from the optic cup (neuroectoderm ) by the continued growth of the outer lip's anterior edge .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 12 -year-old girl you examined in an outreach camp is found to have this abnormality. What is the most common site where the condition is seen ?
mcqs.explanation: The condition depicted in the image is a coloboma of the iris, and the most common site of coloboma is the inferonasal quadrant. A coloboma is a congenital malformation in one of the structures in the eye , such as the iris, retina, choroid, or optic disc, due to the failure of embryonic fissure closure . Coloboma of the uveal tract may be typical (seen in the inferonasal quadrant ) or atypical (occasionally found in other positions ). Typical coloboma is of two types : • Complete : Extends from pupil to optic nerve, causing a corresponding lens indentation. • Incomplete : May involve iris alone, or iris and ciliary body (more common), or iris, ciliary body and a part of choroid. Other embryonic remnants in the eye : • Mittendorf 's dot - Remnant of the anterior end of the hyaloid artery • Bergmeister papilla - Remnant of the posterior end of the hyaloid artery • Persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous (PHPV ) - Failure of fetal vasculature to regress The image below shows a fundoscopy view of persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous.16

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A child was brought with complaints of decreased vision. Fundus examination shows a developmental anomaly as shown below . What is the cause of this anomaly?

options.a: Incomplete closure of the embryonic fissure
options.b: Faulty migration of neural crest cells

mcqs.explanation: The image shows a coloboma of the optic disc, accompanied by a large chorioretinal coloboma located below the optic disc, which is caused by incomplete closure of the embryonic fissure . This developmental anomaly may involve the optic nerve, choroid, retina, and iris. Coloboma of the optic disc can present in two forms: a minor effect often associated with refractive errors like hypermetropia and astigmatism and a fully developed coloboma that appears as a large inferonasal whitish excavation resembling the optic disc. Defective vision and superior visual field defects are typically associated with fully developed coloboma. Additionally , this condition may be associated with chorioretinal coloboma, a congenital anomaly where the developing optic cup fails to fuse completely , leading to abnormal choroidal and retinal development . Note : Faulty migration of neural crest cells results in anterior segment dysgenesis .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: What is the embryological origin of the structure marked in the image?
mcqs.explanation: The lacrimal gland arises from the surface ectoderm .17

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: The optic foramen is situated between the :

options.a: Lesser and greater wings of the sphenoid
options.b: Lesser wing and body of the sphenoid
options.c: Greater wing and body of the sphenoid
options.d: Two roots of the lesser wing of the sphenoid

mcqs.explanation: The optic foramen is situated between the two roots of the lesser wing of the sphenoid . The optic foramen leads into the optic canal, which is formed medially by the body and laterally by the lesser wing of the sphenoid bone, connecting the orbit's apex to the middle cranial fossa. The optic canal transmits the optic nerve with its meningeal coverings; the ophthalmic artery, which is below the nerve, is embedded in its dural sheath , and a few twigs from the sympathetic plexus accompanying the artery.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: During a game, a 26-year-old baseball player is hit in the head by a baseball , which fractures the optic canal. Which of the following pairs of structures is most likely to be damaged ?
mcqs.explanation: 18 In the given clinical scenario, a fracture of the optic canal is most likely to damage the ophthalmic artery and optic nerve, as these are the primary structures passing through it. The optic foramen leads into the optic canal, which is a short cylindrical structure bounded medially by the body and laterally by the lesser wing of the sphenoid bone, connecting the orbit's apex to the middle cranial fossa, serving as a pathway for the aforementioned structures along with its sympathetic plexus . Optic canal fractures, often associated with basilar skull fractures, can lead to optic neuropathy . The intracanalicular and intracranial portion of the optic nerve is most commonly affected in head trauma. Note : The greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid bound the superior orbital fissure .

mcqs.subject: Orthopaedics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of fracture and its management
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a pathognomonic sign of a long bone fracture?
mcqs.explanation: Abnormal mobility in a long bone is a pathognomonic sign of fracture. A fracture is a break in the structural continuity of the bone. Generally , movements occur in the limb only at the joints. If one is able to elicit mobility at locations other than the joints (say in the middle of the arm ), it is a definite sign of a fracture. Crepitus may be felt while doing this. Other features of a fracture include : • Pain13 • Bruising • Swelling • Deformity These can be due to a soft -tissue injury or dislocation as well . Clinically, eliciting abnormal movement or crepitus inflicts more pain. Hence it is no longer recommended.

mcqs.subject: Orthopaedics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of fracture and its management
mcqs.question: Match the following type of fractures with their associated mechanism of force.
mcqs.explanation: The correct match is: Most fractures occur due to a combination of forces , but the dominant mechanism of force is revealed by the type of fracture.Type of fracture Mechanism of fo rce Transverse fractur e Tension Oblique fracture Compression Butterfly fragment Bending Spiral fracture TwistingBased on the continuity of the periosteum , fractures can be complete or incomplete . In complete fractures, the bone is split into two or more fragments and continuity of periosteum is disrupted . It can be:14 • Impacted fracture - The fracture fragments are jammed together and the fracture line is not visible • Comminuted fracture - There is a fracture of more than two fragments • Segmental fracture - A separated fragment is seen in the middle • Avulsion fracture - Breaking of a piece of bone attached to a strong muscle . e.g. olecranon and patella fracture In incomplete fractures, the bone is incompletely split and the periosteum remains in continuity . They include: • Greenstick fractures: The outer cortex breaks and the inner cortex bends causing the bone to buckle like the snapping of a green twig. It is seen in the pediatric population . • Compression fractures: Cancellous bone crumple due to force. This is typically seen in vertebral bodies , calcaneum, and the tibial plateau.

mcqs.subject: Orthopaedics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of fracture and its management
mcqs.question: An elderly woman was brought to the OPD after she slipped and fell from her chair. She is a known case of breast cancer with distant metastasis . The X-ray of the patient is given below . Which of the following statements is false regarding this type of fracture?

options.b: Mirels ' score is used to assess the risk of fracture
options.c: FDG-PET or CT is the gold standard in evaluating bony metastasis
options.d: Pain occurs only after the fracture

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario with a history of trivial trauma, breast cancer, and the X-ray findings are suggestive of a pathological fracture due to bone metastasis . Pain in the case of a pathological fracture usually precedes the fracture. Fractures occur due to: • Trauma • Repetitive stress (stress or fatigue fracture) • Abnormal weakening of the bone (pathological fracture) Pathological fractures are fractures that occur in a weakened bone that has structurally changed due to some condition. They occur either spontaneously or due to minor trauma. The features suggestive of a pathological fracture include : • Pain at the site before the fracture • Multiple recent fractures • Elderly patient • History of primary malignancy • Unusual fracture pattern (Banana fracture - transverse fracture through an abnormal area of bone, similar to breaking a segment from a banana )15 FDG-PET or CT is the gold standard in evaluating bony metastases . The risk of fracture in metastatic bone lesions is assessed using Mirels' score. A Mirels's score > 8 warrants a prophylactic fixation. Management of pathological fracture is based on the causative lesion and survival of the patient .Mirel's criteria Score 1 2 3 Site Upper li mb Lower li mb Peri-trochanteri c Pain Mild Moderat e Functional Lesion Blastic Mixed Lytic Size <1/3 1/3 to 2/ >2

mcqs.subject: Orthopaedics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of fracture and its management
mcqs.question: All of the following conditions can cause a pathological fracture, except :
mcqs.explanation: Fabry's disease does not cause pathological fractures. It presents with angiokeratomas and acroparasthesias. Pathological fractures are fractures that occur in a weakened bone that has structurally changed due to some condition. They occur either spontaneously or due to minor trauma. In Gaucher's disease , there is a deficiency of glucocerebrosidase . This leads to an accumulation of lipid-laden macrophages in the bone tissue , weakening the bone and causing fractures. Osteogenesis imperfecta is an autosomal dominant disorder that occurs most commonly due to mutation in the COL1A and COL2A genes . This results in the abnormal formation of type 1 collagen . Since type 1 collagen is mainly present in the bone, the patient presents with repeated16 fractures with no or minimal trauma. Hyperparathyroidism can cause severe bone resorption leading to bone pains and pathological fracture. Overall, osteoporosis is the most common reason for pathological fractures. Below the age of 20 , the common causes of pathological fracture are benign bone tumors and cysts .

mcqs.subject: Orthopaedics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of fracture and its management
mcqs.question: You are working as a medical officer in the Indian army. An army recruit presents to you with complaints of pain in the right foot. He joined his training 6 months back. His X-ray is given below . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and the X-ray showing a fracture of the 2nd metatarsal are suggestive of a March fracture. It is a type of stress fracture. Stress fractures (or fatigue fractures) occur in a normal bone that is subjected to chronic repetitive stress. This initiates a bone remodeling process . When resorption occurs faster than replacement , the bone becomes liable to fracture. Such fractures are typically seen in athletes , dancers, or military personnel who have a strenuous exercise regimen. Common sites for stress fractures include : • Metatarsals (especially the second , march fracture) • Calcaneum • Navicular • Distal shaft of the fibula (runner's fracture) • Tibial shaft • Patella • Femoral neck MRI is the investigation of choice to diagnose stress fractures. It can visualize lower -grade stress injuries before X-ray changes appear. A bone scan is the investigation of choice when multiple sites have stress fractures. Most stress fractures are managed using an elastic bandage and avoidance of painful activity until the lesion heals . Stress fracture of the femoral neck should be managed by internal fixation as a prophylactic measure . The image below shows a stress fracture:17

mcqs.subject: Orthopaedics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of fracture and its management
mcqs.question: In which of the following conditions does the bone heal by increased callus formation?
mcqs.explanation: Increased callus formation is seen with flexibly fixed fractures. Fracture heals through direct union (primary bone healing) or callus formation (secondary bone healing). • Direct union: This occurs when the fracture site is absolutely stable . This is seen in a fracture held by a metal plate with absolute stability and in cases of impacted fracture in cancellous bones. There is no stimulus for callus formation. Osteoblastic new bone formation occurs directly between the fracture fragments. • Callus formation: This occurs when the fracture is not fixed rigidly. The healing proceeds through 5 stages : • Hematoma formation • Inflammation • Soft callus formation • Hard callus formation • Remodeling Healing by callus ensures mechanical strength as the movement and stress make the callus grow stronger.18 The image below shows callus formation:

mcqs.subject: Orthopaedics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of fracture and its management
mcqs.question: A teenager is brought to the casualty after sustaining a wrist injury during a sports meet . His X-ray is given below . The orthopedic surgeon tries to reduce the fracture fragments by using traction on soft tissues around the bones. What is this technique known as?
mcqs.explanation: The technique which uses traction on the soft tissue around the bones to reduce the fracture fragments is known as ligamentotaxis . The given X-ray shows a fracture of the radial styloid process (Chauffeur 's fracture or Hutchinson fracture). Reduction of the fracture is done to ensure normal alignment and adequate apposition of the bone fragments. There are two methods of reduction : • Closed reduction : The fracture is reduced under appropriate anesthesia and muscle relaxation. Closed reduction of fracture relies on indirect fragment alignment utilizing the pull of the soft tissue envelope (ligaments and capsules ), which is known as ligamentotaxis .19 • Open reduction : Operative reduction of the fracture under direct vision. Option A and C: Callotaxis is callus distraction or distraction osteogenesis . It is used for limb lengthening or filling of large segmental defects in the bone. Option D: Arthrodesis (artificial ankylosis or syndesis ) is the artificial induction of joint ossification between two bones by surgery.

mcqs.subject: Orthopaedics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of fracture and its management
mcqs.question: Hanging cast is used to treat which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: A hanging cast is used to treat the fractured shaft of the humerus. Humerus shaft fracture heals readily with just the external cast as it is usually enough to bring the fragments into alignment. The arm is placed over the lower chest with the elbow at 90\260. A collar and cuff support can be used to maintain the position. The weight of the arm provides continuous traction to the humerus (traction by gravity).After the fracture is reduced , it is important to hold the reduction with some restriction of movements to promote soft -tissue healing and to allow free movement of the unaffected parts. The methods of holding reduction include : • Continuous traction (traction by gravity, skin traction, or skeletal traction) • Cast splintage • Functional bracing • Internal fixation • External fixation

mcqs.subject: Orthopaedics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of fracture and its management
mcqs.question: A cast was applied to a patient with a wrist injury as shown below . What is this cast known as?
mcqs.explanation: 20 The cast applied to a patient in the glass holding position is known as the scaphoid cast. It is used to treat scaphoid fractures. To apply a scaphoid cast, the wrist is held in slight dorsiflexion and the thumb is in abduction and slight flexion as if the glass is being held between the index finger and thumb. It extends from just below the elbow to just proximal to the metacarpal necks of the digits . On the thumb, the cast extends just proximal to the interphalangeal joint. Scaphoid fracture presents with pain and swelling over the radial aspect of the wrist. A fall on an outstretched hand could result in such a fracture. The fracture can be confirmed (when an x-ray does not show a fracture) if there is pain elicited in the anatomical snuff box on the radial border of the wrist. An oblique x-ray of the wrist should be able to show a scaphoid fracture.

mcqs.subject: Orthopaedics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of fracture and its management
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements are true about open fractures?
mcqs.explanation: Open fractures are usually associated with multiple other injuries and compartment syndrome can occur as a complication of open fractures. Open fractures are characterized by a break in the overlying skin and soft tissues . Hence , the fracture fragment is exposed to the external environment. It is usually associated with multiple other injuries. The most common sites involved in open fractures include • Phalanges (Fingers and toes ) • Tibial diaphysis • Distal radius • Ankle Open fractures are more prone to develop an infection , as it's exposed to the external environment . The presence of an open fracture does not prevent the development of compartment syndrome. Major components of management of all open fractures are: • Antibiotic prophylaxis - It should be given as early as possible • Early debridement of the wound and fracture - This includes the following steps : • Excision of the wound margins • Extension of the wound if required • Delivery of the fracture outside the wound for proper examination • Removal of the devitalized tissue • Cleansing of the wound to remove all the foreign materials • Nerves and tendons are usually left alone, but if the wound is clean, a repair can be considered • Wound cover :21 • In Gustilo Type I and II fractures wound cover can be done at the time of debridement (Early wound cover) • Delayed wound cover is usually practiced in Type III fractures • Fracture stabilization - The method of stabilization depends on the degree of contamination, amount of soft tissue damage , and time from the injury to operation. • External fixation is used as a temporary measure if there is a delay in wound cover • If definitive wound cover can be achieved at the time of debridement and there is no significant contamination, then an open fracture can be managed as same as a closed injury

mcqs.subject: Orthopaedics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of fracture and its management
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old man presents with a fracture of the right tibia following an RTA . On examination , the wound is highly contaminated and appears as shown below . His distal pulses are felt well . According to the Gustilo -Anderson classification , this injury would be classified as type :
mcqs.explanation: This open fracture will be classified as Type IIIB on Gustilo -Anderson's classification due to the extensive wound (>10 cm), high contamination, very severe loss of soft tissue cover, and intact vascularity. A fracture where the skin and soft tissues are breached is known as an open fracture (or a compound fracture). Gustilo and Anderson's classification is the most commonly followed classification for open fractures. Open fractures with an arterial injury that requires repair will be classified as IIIC , irrespective of the size of the soft -tissue wound .

mcqs.subject: Orthopaedics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of fracture and its management
mcqs.question: You are the intern on duty and you receive patients who have been in a road traffic accident . For which of the following patients will you urgently call the orthopaedic resident on call?

options.b: Patient with a fractured arm with capillary refill time of less than 3 seconds in his fingers
options.c: Patient with a fractures arm with a 10 cm long incision over the arm
options.d: Patient with a fractured arm with capillary refill time of 5 seconds in his fingers

mcqs.explanation: Capillary refill time of more than 3 seconds indicates inadequate limb perfusion . It is a surgical emergency and could be due to either vascular injury by direct trauma or compartment syndrome. Hence an orthopedic intervention will be needed urgently . All other patients will also need an orthopedic intervention, however, the blood flow should be restored at the earliest .

mcqs.subject: Orthopaedics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of fracture and its management
mcqs.question: An industrial worker was rushed to casualty after he accidentally got his leg stuck in a machine. On examination, he was found to have an open fracture as shown below . He was urgently taken up for wound debridement and was considered for primary closure . It can be performed in all of the following conditions, except :

options.a: If injury to debridement interval < 12 hours
options.d: Wound margin can be closed without tension

mcqs.explanation: When there is impaired nerve supply , primary closure of open fracture is not recommended . Primary closure of open fracture is the closure of the wound by direct skin suturing during the index procedure (first debridement ). In general , primary closure of wounds of Gustilo type I and II fractures can be done at the time of debridement . In Gustilo type IIIA fractures, some surgeons delay closure until a second -look procedure is performed. In most cases of Gustilo type IIIB and IIIC injuries, a delayed closure is practiced . Important criteria for primary closure : • The patient ' s general condition should be stable22 • Injury to debridement interval is < 12 hours • All necrotic material must have been removed • Stable fixation can be achieved either by internal or external fixation • Normal circulation • Intact nerve supply • The wound skin margins can be closed without tension • There should be no multisystem injuries

mcqs.subject: Orthopaedics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of fracture and its management
mcqs.question: In which of the following fractures is surgical management necessary for optimum functional results ?
mcqs.explanation: Surgical management is necessary for optimum functional results in Monteggia fracture (fracture of the ulnar shaft with concomitant dislocation of the radial head ). While the other listed injuries may necessitate surgery in certain situations , conservative treatment for Monteggia fracture yields poor results . Fractures in which surgical treatment will be needed to obtain an optimal result include : • Displaced intraarticular fractures • Unstable fractures after failed conservative management • Major avulsion fractures after failed conservative management • Displaced pathologic fractures • Fractures in which conservative treatment is known to provide poor functional results , such as femoral neck fractures, Galeazzi fracture-dislocations , and Monteggia fracture-dislocations • Displaced physeal injuries with high-risk for growth arrest (Salter-Harris types III and IV ) • Nonunions, especially malreduced ones, after failed conservative or operative management

mcqs.subject: Orthopaedics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of fracture and its management
mcqs.question: All of the following are common indications for the procedure shown below , except :
mcqs.explanation: The image shows external fixation using an external fixator. Type 1 open fracture is not a common indication for external fixation. External fixation is holding the fracture using transfixing screws that pass through the bone above and below the fracture and are connected to each other by rigid bars or an external frame. mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: How many base pairs the human genome is made of?
mcqs.explanation: The human genome is the complete set of nucleic acid sequences for humans and is made up of 3.2 billion base pairs. It is encoded as DNA within the 23 chromosomes (haploid ). In 2007, a multinational project called Encyclopedia of DNA Elements (ENCODE ) concluded that about 80% of the human genome does not code for the proteins . However, they allow for the binding of proteins or are involved in the regulation of gene expression , in a cell type -specific fashion. They are known as functional non-protein-coding genes .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following describes the non-coding regulatory RNAs?

options.a: Transcribed from protein-coding regions of DNA and translated to regulatory proteins
options.b: Transcribed from protein-coding regions of DNA but never translated
options.c: Transcribed from non-protein-coding regions of DNA and translated to regulatory proteins
options.d: Transcribed from non-protein-coding regions of DNA but never translated

mcqs.explanation: The non-coding regulatory RNAs are the functional non-protein-coding regions of the DNA, which are transcribed to RNA but are never translated into proteins . The two important types of non-coding regulatory RNAs are the micro RNA (miRNA ) and the long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs). These RNAs play an important role in the regulation of gene expression .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the study of heritable changes in gene expression that are not caused by alterations in DNA sequence?
mcqs.explanation: Epigenetics is the branch of molecular biology that deals with the study of heritable changes in gene function not involving changes in the DNA sequence . These heritable changes involve factors that mediate processes such as: • Histone organization • DNA methylation • Chromatin organization These in turn regulate the genomic organization and gene expression in a cell -type -specific fashion. The dysregulation of these epigenomic factors plays a major role in the development of malignancy. Green tea catechins have been reported to modulate epigenetic processes . They can reverse DNA methylation of tumor suppressor genes and increase the transcription of these genes .13

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Micro-RNA are involved during which of the following stages ?
mcqs.explanation: Micro-RNAs (miRNA ) act during the post -transcriptional stage . It is a type of non-coding RNA. The primary function of miRNA is to modulate the translation of target mRNAs into their corresponding proteins . After the target RNA is transcribed from its gene (post -transcriptional), the miRNA may either induce mRNA cleavage or repress its translation. This is referred to as gene silencing . Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) are short RNA sequences that can be introduced experimentally into cells . They have functions similar to endogenous miRNA (serve as substrates for the Dicer enzyme and interact with the RNA-induced silencing complex ). They may have a therapeutic role in silencing certain oncogenes .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false about microRNAs ?

options.b: They are involved in cell differentiation and carcinogenesis
options.c: Mature forms of microRNAs are single stranded
options.d: They can suppress tumor suppressor genes

mcqs.explanation: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small noncoding, single -stranded RNAs. They are approximately 22 nucleotides in length . MicroRNAs mediate inhibition of messenger RNA (mRNA ) translation through the action of the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC ). They control normal cell growth , differentiation , and cell survival . miRNA can be of 2 types : • Tumour-suppressive miRNAs - decrease the translation of oncogenic mRNAs • Onco-miRNAs - suppress tumor-suppressor genes Other noncoding RNAs include : • piwi-interacting RNAs (piRNAs) - involved in post -transcriptional gene silencing • snoRNAs - involved in maturation of rRNA , assembly of ribosomes and noncoding RNAs • lncRNAs - regulate the activity of chromatin 'writers', which modify histones and control gene expression

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of cell injury?
mcqs.explanation: Hypoxia is the most common cause of cell injury. Causes of cell injury include : • Hypoxia • Physical agents • Chemical agents and drugs • Infectious agents • Immunologic reactions • Genetic abnormalities14 • Nutritional imbalances The mechanism of hypoxic cell injury is reduced oxidative respiration. The most common cause of hypoxia is ischemia. Hypoxia-inducible factor 1 (HIF-1) is a transcription factor with protective effects against hypoxic injury such as: • Promotion of blood vessel formation • Stimulation of cell -survival pathways • Enhancement of anaerobic glycolysis The cells most sensitive to hypoxia are neurons. The most sensitive neurons include : • Pyramidal neurons of the hippocampus (especially , area CA1, also known as Sommer's sector ) • Cerebellar Purkinje cells • Pyramidal neurons in the cerebral cortex The cells most resistant to hypoxia are fibroblasts.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false ?

options.a: Atrophy is a type of reversible cell injury
options.b: Plasma membrane blebbing occurs in reversible cell injury
options.c: On removal of stimulus , necrosis can be reversed
options.d: Chronic sublethal stimulus can cause cellular aging

mcqs.explanation: On removal of stimulus , necrosis cannot be reversed. It is an irreversible cell injury. Cellular adaptations are the reversible responses where the cells achieve an altered steady state in response to physiologic or some pathologic stimuli. They can be reversed if the stimulus causing stress or injury is removed. These cellular adaptations include : • Hypertrophy • Hyperplasia • Atrophy • Metaplasia Chronic sublethal stimuli are unable to cause cell death but may lead to certain changes in cells , such as: • Intracellular accumulations • Pathological calcifications • Cellular aging15

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which among the following is not a feature of reversible cell injury?

options.a: Large amorphous densities in the mitochondria
options.d: Detachment of ribosomes from granular ER

mcqs.explanation: Small amorphous densities are seen in the mitochondria in reversible cell injury. The following changes occur in reversible cell injury: • Cellular swelling - earliest change • ATP depletion leads to sodium-potassium pump failure • Na and water accumulate within the cell causing cellular swelling • Fatty change - • Seen in cells involved in or dependent on fat metabolism (liver hepatocytes and myocardial cells ) • Light microscopy - no noticeable changes • Ultrastructural findings - • Mitochondrial swelling and small amorphous densities • Plasma membrane blebs • Swelling of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) • Detachment of ribosomes from granular ER • Nuclear changes like disaggregation of granular and fibrillar filaments Note : The formation of large amorphous densities in the mitochondria is a feature of irreversible injury.16

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which is the most important light microscopic feature of irreversible cell injury?

options.b: Cell membrane blebs and loss of microvilli
options.d: Nuclear changes like pyknosis and karyolysis

mcqs.explanation: Nuclear changes like pyknosis, karyorrhexis, and karyolysis are features of irreversible cell injury visible on light microscopy. The ultrastructural findings visible on electron microscopy include : • Large amorphous floccular densities in mitochondria • Cell membrane blebs and loss of microvilli • Ribosomal detachment from endoplasmic reticulum

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Thrombosis is initiated by:
mcqs.explanation: Thrombosis is initiated by endothelial injury. Thrombosis is is the formation of a blood clot inside a blood vessel , obstructing the flow of blood through the circulatory system . Three primary abnormalities, often referred to as Virchow triad, are known to induce thrombosis. They include: • Endothelial injury - most important factor • Stasis or turbulent blood flow • Hypercoagulability of the blood

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about cellular adaptations is correct?

options.a: Hyperplasia involves synthesis of intracellular components
options.b: Atrophy is defined as decrease in cell size
options.c: Atrophy is the decrease in number and size of cells
options.d: Metaplasia is an irreversible replacement of a cell by another cell type

mcqs.explanation: 17 Atrophy is a reduction in the size of an organ or tissue due to a decrease in cell size and number. Cellular adaptations are reversible changes in the size, number, phenotype , metabolic activity, or functions of cells in response to changes in their environment. There are 4 types : • Hypertrophy - • Increase in organ size due to an increase in the size of cells • Involves synthesis and assembly of intracellular structural components • Hyperplasia - • Increase in organ size due to an increase in the number of cells • It is due to division and proliferation of stem cells • Atrophy - reduction in organ size due to a decrease in cell size and number. • Metaplasia - one differentiated cell type (epithelial or mesenchymal ) is replaced by another cell type

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Both physiological hyperplasia and hypertrophy are simultaneously seen in which of the following individuals?

options.a: A 24-year-old man vigorously training for an athletic race
options.b: A 35-year-old woman regularly taking combined oral contraceptive pills
options.c: A 50-year-old man with proliferation of liver cells following transplantation
options.d: A 24-year-old pregnant woman at 22 weeks of gestation

mcqs.explanation: Physiological hypertrophy and hyperplasia can be simultaneously seen in the uterus during pregnancy. In early pregnancy, uterine growth is due to hyperplasia of uterine smooth muscle cells ; however, the predominant growth of the uterus during pregnancy occurs after mid-gestation , by way of stretch \037induced myometrial hypertrophy . Simultaneous physiological hypertrophy and hyperplasia also occur in the female breast during puberty and pregnancy. Option A: Enlargement of skeletal muscles in athletes is an example of physiological hypertrophy . Option B: Combined oral contraceptive pills causing endometrial hyperplasia is an example of pathological hyperplasia . Option C: Following transplantation of a liver lobe , the remaining liver cells proliferate so that the organ grows back to its original size (compensatory hyperplasia ).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which among the following do not usually undergo hyperplasia ?
mcqs.explanation: Skeletal muscle and heart muscle usually undergo hypertrophy , not hyperplasia . Examples of physiologic hyperplasia : • Female breast during puberty and pregnancy (hormonal hyperplasia ) • Uterine smooth muscle during early pregnancy • Compensatory hyperplasia of liver cells after partial resection Examples of pathologic hyperplasia : • Endometrial hyperplasia • Benign prostatic hyperplasia

mcqs.question: Which of the following timelines would be included in the perinatal period as per WHO?

options.a: 37th week of gestation to 28 days after birth
options.b: 20th week of gestation to 7 days after birth
options.c: 28th week of gestation to 28 days after birth
options.d: 22nd week of gestation to 7 days after birth

mcqs.explanation: The WHO states that the perinatal period commences at 22 completed weeks and ends at seven completed days after birth - 154 days. It corresponds to when the fetus weighs 500g or more. This definition is not to be confused with the period used for the calculation of the perinatal mortality rate (PMR). To calculate the PMR, a fetal weight above 1000 g is considered , which is achieved at 28 weeks of gestation . Therefore, for all statistical purposes , international comparisons, and calculation of perinatal mortality rate, the period from the 28th week of life is considered .10 Perinatal period : from the 22nd week . Perinatal mortality rate calculation: from the 28th week . The neonatal period is defined as the first 28 days after birth. Infancy is defined as the first year of life . The image below shows various time periods . Only the time period for perinatal mortality and the perinatal period are different as shown in the image. For others, corresponding mortality rates are calculated using the same time periods shown.

mcqs.question: You would classify a baby as post -term if it is born after ________
mcqs.explanation: Post-term infants are those born after 42 completed weeks of gestation , as calculated from the mother's last menstrual period , regardless of weight at birth.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of Neonatology and Routine Newborn Care
mcqs.question: You would classify a baby as a very low birth weight baby if the weight of the baby is found to be less than _____ kg.
mcqs.explanation: A very low birth weight baby is one whose birth weight is <1.5 Kg . They are often premature (<37 weeks of gestation ). A low birth weight baby is one whose birth weight is <2.5 Kg . An extremely low birth weight baby is one whose birth weight is <1 kg.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of Neonatology and Routine Newborn Care
mcqs.question: Reena, a 34-year-old lady with gestation diabetes mellitus delivers an LGA baby at 37 weeks . What would the birth weight of this child be?
mcqs.explanation: Infants with birth weight greater than the 90th percentile for their gestational age are called large for gestational age (LGA) babies.11 Maternal diabetes and obesity are predisposing factors for LGA babies. They have a higher incidence of: • Birth injuries: • Brachial plexus injury • Phrenic nerve injury • Cephalohematomas • Hypoglycemia • Polycythemia • Congenital heart disease

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of Neonatology and Routine Newborn Care
mcqs.question: As the intern assisting in the labor room, you are tasked with administering Vitamin K to the term newborns with no complications . Which of the following dose and route would you use for administration?
mcqs.explanation: All newborn infants are to be administered vitamin K at a dose of 0.5–1 mg intramuscularly, to prevent hemorrhagic disease of the newborn (HDN). However, for newborns with vitamin K deficiency , the dose of vitamin K administered is 1–5 mg intravenously.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of Neonatology and Routine Newborn Care
mcqs.question: A term neonate born by normal vaginal delivery is diagnosed with hypothermia . Which of the following is not a physiological response for heat regulation in this baby?

options.b: Breakdown of brown fat with noradrenaline secretion

mcqs.explanation: Neonates do not generate heat by shivering. Heat production in neonates happens by increasing the metabolic rate and oxygen consumption by releasing norepinephrine , which results in non-shivering thermogenesis through beta -oxidation of brown fat. This sympathetic surge also causes cutaneous vasoconstriction.12 Increased physical activity - crying, increased body movements, and muscular activity also contribute to thermogenesis . Preterm and small-for-gestational -age (SGA) infants have scanty brown fat stores .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of Neonatology and Routine Newborn Care
mcqs.question: You are conducting the routine newborn assessment of a 2.3 kg baby born 10 minutes back. You would classify the neonate as having cold stress if you notice the body temperature to be:
mcqs.explanation: A temperature of 36.0 to 36.4\260C categorizes a neonate as having cold stress . An infant's normal body temperature is 36.5 to 37.5 \260C. It is measured in the apex of the baby's axilla by holding the thermometer for at least 3 minutes . Hypothermia is an axillary temperature of <36.5 \260C. • Cold stress : 36.0 to 36.4 \260C • Moderate hypothermia : 32 to 35.9 \260C • Severe hypothermia : <32 \260C Hyperthermia is an axillary temperature of >37.5 \260C.

mcqs.chapter: Basics of Neonatology and Routine Newborn Care
mcqs.question: A 24-year-old primigravida delivers a preterm baby at 33 weeks of gestation with a birth weight of 2 kg. She is advised to hold her child as shown below . Which of the following statements about this method is false ?

options.b: Safety and thermal protection is equivalent to incubators
options.c: Reduces severe morbidity in the newborns
options.d: Should be performed only by the mother

mcqs.explanation: Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC ) can be carried out by the mother or any other caregiver. KMC was introduced for the prevention of neonatal hypothermia in low birth weight / premature newborns. It has 4 components — • Skin -to-skin positioning of the newborn on the mother's chest . • Adequate nutrition through breastfeeding . • Early discharge and ambulatory care. • Support for mother and family for child care. Evidence shows that- • It is as good as incubators, in terms of safety and thermal protection (measured by mortality) • Reduces severe morbidity by way of facilitating breastfeeding • Humanization of neonatal care • Promoted bonding between mother and child Eligibility criteria for KMC : It is indicated for all hemodynamically stable low birth weight babies. Short sessions of KMC can be initiated in babies on medical treatment like IV fluids or oxygen therapy . Initiation of KMC can vary with the birth weight of the baby. • Birth weight <1200 g - It may take days to weeks for initiation of KMC • Birth weight =1200 -1800 g - Only a few days may be taken before KMC initiation13 • Birth weight >1800 g - KMC can be initiated immediately after birth All mothers without any serious illness can provide KMC . Positioning for KMC : The baby is placed between the mother's breast in an upright position. The hips are abducted and flexed in the frog position and the arms are also flexed . The abdomen of the baby should be at the level of the mother's epigastrium . In this position, the mother's breathing would stimulate the baby and prevent the development of apnea. The duration of KMC should be gradually increased from short sessions of more than one hour to 24 hours a day. KMC is not necessary once the baby attains 2500 g of weight or 37 weeks of gestation . Note : Incubatory care, feeding via nasal catheter , and prevention of infection are part of intensive care for low birthweight babies.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of Neonatology and Routine Newborn Care
mcqs.question: While examining a healthy term neonate , you notice that the baby passes greenish -black colored stools . This color is due to -
mcqs.explanation: The greenish -black color of the first stool in the newborn is due to biliverdin. Meconium is a dark , sticky material that is normally present in the intestine at birth and passed in the feces after birth. It is detected in the ileum at about 70–85 days of fetal life and begins to fill the colon and lower ileum late in the 4th month of gestation . The greenish color of the meconium is the consequence of the bile pigments excreted by the biliary tract. The main component16 responsible for the greenish color of the meconium is biliverdin (a pigment formed from the oxidation of bilirubin). Up to the 22nd week of gestation , the intestinal content is not greenish and for this reason, fetal defecation would not stain the amniotic fluid . The production of biliverdin starts over the next few weeks or at a time closer to labor, probably due to a biochemical switch related to the bilirubin oxidation system . Bilirubin is responsible for the yellow color of the stools . Neonates do not harbor gut flora at birth.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Basics of Neonatology and Routine Newborn Care
mcqs.question: When does the parachute reflex disappear ?

options.c: At birth and reappears at 9 months

mcqs.explanation: The parachute reflex has its onset at 7–8 months of age . It is fully developed by 10 -11 months of age and remains throughout life . It can be evoked by holding the infant's trunk and then suddenly lowering the infant as if he or she were falling. The arms will spontaneously extend to break the infant's fall. This reflex is a prerequisite to walking.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics

mcqs.question: A 6-day old infant is being examined. While checking the reflexes , a brisk Moro's reflex is noted . Which of the following conditions is a likely cause for this?
mcqs.explanation: A brisk Moro reflex can be seen in neonates with hypoglycemia . In hypoglycemic babies, there is an activation of the autonomic system , which results in jitteriness . Newborns often exhibit this as an exaggerated Moro reflex . The Moro reflex is a primitive reflex that is very sensitive to the infant's level of alertness . It is elicited by supporting the infant in the semierect position and allowing the infant's head to fall backward onto the examiner's hand. An animated gif of normal response to Moro's reflex where there is symmetrical extension and abduction of the upper extremities , followed by flexion of the upper extremities is shown below17 The Moro reflex disappears by 6 months of age in normal infants. Absent Moro reflex : caused by significant generalized disturbance of the CNS • Stage III HIE • Kernicterus Asymmetric Moro reflex : feature of the root, plexus , or nerve disease • Fractured clavicle • Brachial plexus injury (Erb's palsy ) • Hemiparesis Brisk Moro reflex : • Neonatal hypoglycemia • Can also be a normal variant in healthy infants • Stage I HIE Exaggerated , stereotyped , non-habituating Moro reflex is a feature of severe bilateral intrauterine cerebral disturbance , perhaps because of the release of the brain stem from inhibitory cortical influences . It is seen in conditions such as the following : • Hydranencephaly • Severe micrencephaly Moro reflex in different stages of hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE): • Stage I HIE (mild): Brisk • Stage II HIE (moderate ): Weak/incomplete • Stage III HIE (severe): Absent Option A: In kernicterus, there is a deposition of unconjugated bilirubin in the basal ganglia and brain stem . Hence , the Moro reflex is absent Option C: In stage III HIE, the muscles are flaccid and the infant is comatose . Thus, the Moro reflex is absent. Option D: Erb's palsy results from an injury to the brachial plexus . So, the reflex is absent on the side of injury as the nerve supplying the muscles involved (efferent of the reflex ) is affected .

mcqs.question: You are demonstrating findings in a pediatric OSCE examination on a 4-day old neonate . On turning the baby's head to the left , you obtain the finding as shown below . At what age does this reflex normally disappear ?
mcqs.explanation: Asymmetric tonic neck reflex (ATNR ) disappears by 6 months postnatally . The tonic neck reflex is produced by manually rotating the infant's head to 1 side and observing for the characteristic fencing posture (extension of the arm on the side to which the face is rotated and flexion of the contralateral arm ).18 An obligatory tonic neck response , in which the infant becomes "stuck" in the fencing posture , is always abnormal and implies a CNS disorder.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Fundoscopic evaluation in an HIV patient showed CMV retinitis. He was started on intravenous foscarnet, a highly ionized drug. Which of the following statements is true about the drug?

options.b: Can cross the blood brain barrier easily

mcqs.explanation: Highly ionized drugs like foscarnet are mainly excreted by the kidneys. They are not reabsorbed from the renal tubules and are hence excreted unchanged by glomerular filtration. Dose reduction is necessary in renal impairment to avoid the accumulation of the drug and associated toxicity . The non-ionized forms of weak acids and bases undergo tubular reabsorption. Option B: The blood-brain barrier limits the entry of ionized, non-lipid soluble drugs. Option C: A drug is more readily absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract when it is in its unionized, more lipophilic form. Option D: As the ionized form has low lipid solubility , it cannot penetrate cell membranes easily .13

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Alkalinization of the urine is done in case of toxicity with which of the following substances ?
mcqs.explanation: Alkalinization of the urine is done in barbiturate poisoning. When the urine is alkaline, weakly acidic drugs like barbiturates are present in highly ionized form and excreted more rapidly. When the tubular urine is made more alkaline, weak acids like barbiturates become highly ionized and are excreted to a greater extent . Similarly, acidification of urine increases the excretion of weak bases . This property is used in the management of drug overdose.Drug Treatment of overdose Weak acids(e.g., phenobarbit al, aspirin) Alkalinization of urine withso dium bicarbonate Weak bases (e.g., amphetami ne) Acidification of urine witham monium chloride

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: When the pH = pKa of a drug, which of the following statements is true?

options.a: Concentration of the drug is 50% ionic and 50 % non-ionic
options.b: Concentration of the drug is 90% ionic and 10 % non-ionic
options.c: Concentration of the drug is 75 % ionic and 25 % non-ionic
options.d: Concentration of the drug is 25% ionic and 75 % non-ionic

mcqs.explanation: When the pH = pKa of a drug, the concentration of the drug is 50% ionic and 50% non-ionic. pKa is defined as the pH at which a drug exists as 50% ionized (hydrophilic ) and 50% unionized (lipophilic ). For e.g., phenobarbitone is an acidic drug with a pKa of 7.2. At a pH of 7.2, 50% will be unionized. In a more basic plasma (pH=7.4), a lesser fraction (around 40%) will be unionized. Small changes in pH near pKa of a drug may cause large variations in the degree of ionization.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: In a patient with nephrotic syndrome, drug toxicity is least likely with which of the following drugs?
mcqs.explanation: In a patient with nephrotic syndrome, drug toxicity is least likely with morphine. Acidic drugs generally bind to plasma albumin while basic drugs bind to alpha-1 acid glycoprotein . Nephrotic syndrome reduces plasma albumin levels , therefore there is a decrease in the protein-bound drug fraction and an increase in the free form, resulting in drug toxicity . This is less likely with drugs having low plasma protein binding such as morphine (only around 35%). Efavirenz, diazepam, and valproate have a very high plasma protein binding of >90% and predominantly bind to albumin and are associated with toxicity in hypoalbuminemia .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: What does time for peak plasma concentration (Tmax ) indicate ?
mcqs.explanation: The time for peak plasma concentration (Tmax ) indicates the rate at which the drug is absorbed from the administered site . It depends on both the administered site and the drug formulation.14 This is used to determine the timing of the administration of hypnotics with respect to sleep timings. A hypnotic with a higher rate of absorption might be preferred to induce sleep at a shorter latency as the target concentration can be achieved earlier.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: The pharmacokinetics of an experimental drug is being studied . If its apparent volume of distribution is 6L /kg, which of the following is true regarding its distribution?
mcqs.explanation: In the present case, the volume of distribution of the drug is 6L /kg (420 L in a normal adult with reference weight 70kg) which is very high when compared to the total body water of 42L . Therefore, it can be implied that the drug is having high sequestration in tissues . The apparent volume of distribution (Vd) is an imaginary volume throughout which the drug is distributed if the plasma concentration remains constant throughout . Vd = Dose administered IV / plasma concentration The difference in the volume of distribution based on drug type : • Low Vd • Restricted to the intravascular compartment • Seen in drugs with high molecular weight (e.g., heparin) or high protein binding (e.g., warfarin - 9.8L) • Medium Vd • Lipid insoluble drugs (e.g., gentamicin - 20L ) do not enter the cells and are distributed in the extracellular fluid volume • Small water-soluble molecules (e.g., ethanol - 42L ) are distributed in the total body water • High Vd • Sequestered and accumulated in the tissues • Small lipophilic molecules (e.g., chloroquine - 13000L )

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following parameters is used to assess the extent of drug absorption in a plasma concentration vs. time graph?
mcqs.explanation: The area under the curve of plasma concentration vs. time curve gives the extent of absorption which is calculated by the trapezoidal rule. The following image shows a plasma concentration vs. time graph:15 Two drugs may have the same rate of absorption but a different extent of absorption or bioavailability. The factors upon which the extent of drug absorption depends are: • Lipophilicity - If too lipophilic (e.g., acyclovir), the drug is not soluble enough to cross the water layer adjacent to the cell . • Hydrophilicity - If too hydrophilic (e.g., atenolol ), the drug cannot cross the lipid cell membrane.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is true about first-order kinetics?

options.a: A constant amount of drug is eliminated in unit time
options.b: The half life increases with an increase in dose
options.c: The rate of elimination is constant
options.d: The rate of elimination is proportional to the plasma concentration

mcqs.explanation: The rate of elimination is proportional to plasma concentration in first-order kinetics.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: You would consider administering a loading dose for a patient if the drug has
mcqs.explanation: The volume of distribution of the drug determines the loading dose of the drug. Loading dose is a relatively large dose of the drug given initially to rapidly achieve the target plasma concentration. It is given by the formula Loading Dose = Vol. of Distribution x Desired Steady -state plasma Concentration. The bioavailability determines the route of administration. Though bioavailability may affect the dose necessary, it will not be the primary factor considered during the calculation of the loading dose . Option A: Clearance is used to determine the maintenance dose . Maintenance dose = Clearance x Desired Steady -state plasma concentration. Options C and D: Plasma half-life primarily determines the frequency of dosing.16

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following drugs approach zero-order kinetics at higher therapeutic levels ?
mcqs.explanation: Phenytoin kinetics changes from first-order to zero-order kinetics at higher therapeutic levels . True zero-order kinetics is shown only by ethanol . Some drugs have first-order kinetics at low plasma concentrations while at higher plasma concentration (within therapeutic range ), the mechanism for elimination gets saturated and they change over to zero-order kinetics. Drugs that show early saturation kinetics include : • Warfarin • Aspirin • Theophylline • Verapamil • Fluoxetine • Phenytoin Some drugs show zero-order kinetics at much higher (non-therapeutic / toxic) levels .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following routes of administration will not bypass hepatic first-pass metabolism ?
mcqs.explanation: Hepatic first-pass metabolism occurs in drugs administered via the oral route. When drugs are given orally, they are absorbed in the intestine and reach the liver through the portal vein. During this process , the drug is acted on by enzymes of the liver and intestine . Additionally , the liver may excrete part of the drug in the bile, further reducing the bioavailability. This is called the first-pass metabolism . In all the other routes , the drug directly enters systemic circulation without reaching the liver. Note : Bioavailability is the fraction of an administered dose of unchanged drug that reaches the systemic circulation. Hence , the bioavailability of a drug administered intravenously (I.V ) is 100 %. It is neither subjected to the first-pass metabolism as in the oral route nor does it depend on local factors as in subcutaneous , intramuscular, or transdermal.

mcqs.question: Sulphonamides undergo which of the following metabolic reactions?

mcqs.question: All of the following can cause lupus -like syndromes except :
mcqs.explanation: Penicillin is not associated with a lupus -like syndrome. mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A patient on long-term anticoagulation therapy with warfarin would need an increased dose when coadministered with which of the following drugs?
mcqs.explanation: A patient on long-term anticoagulation therapy with warfarin would need an increased dose when coadministered with rifampicin. This is because rifampicin is a potent microsomal enzyme18 inducer and can decrease the effect of warfarin . Rifampicin induces CYP3A and CYP2D6 enzymes . Enzyme inducers: • CYP3A • Carbamazepine • Phenobarbitone (CYP2B1) • Rifampicin (CYP2D6) • Phenytoin • Glucocorticoids • CYP2E1 • Isoniazid • Chronic alcoholism Note : Isoniazid is an inducer for CYP2E1 but an inhibitor for CYP3A4

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Homeostasis is called as dynamic equilibrium because ______

options.a: All variables are given equal importance
options.b: Can achieve a constancy in extreme environmental challenge
options.c: The set -point for all homeostatic variables is always fixed
options.d: Body maintains an internal balance within fluctuating limits

mcqs.explanation: Homeostasis is called dynamic equilibrium because the body maintains an internal balance within fluctuating limits. It describes the maintenance of nearly constant conditions in the internal environment despite changes in the outside world. A number of variables such as body temperature , blood sugar levels , blood pH, etc . are regulated within a range of values (homeostatic ranges) and not at fixed values. These variables are not given equal importance. There is a hierarchy of importance so that the constancy of certain variables may be altered markedly to maintain others within their normal range. For example , respiratory or metabolic compensation to maintain blood pH. The disruption of homeostasis either due to extreme environmental challenge or a breakdown of internal homeostatic mechanisms is termed as a disease .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which is a component of homeostatic control system ?
mcqs.explanation: Stimulus , receptor and effector are all components of a homeostatic control system . Components of homeostasis include : • Stimulus - It is a detectable change in the internal or external environment, such as change in temperature . • Receptor - It detects environmental changes . • Integrating centre • Effector - It is an organ or cell that acts in response to a stimulus .11

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Feedback regulation is seen in ______

options.a: The increased heart rate that occurs in an athlete just before a sprint begins
options.b: Smell of food triggers secretion of salivary and gastric juices
options.c: An increase in insulin before glucose absorption has raised blood glucose levels
options.d: The increased heart rate in response to a decrease in blood pressure

mcqs.explanation: Feedback regulation is seen in the increased heart rate in response to a decrease in blood pressure . This is because , in feedback regulation , the homeostatic response (increased heart rate) occurs after the change (decrease in blood pressure ) has occurred. On the other hand, in feedforward regulation , the homeostatic responses take place before the change has occurred. This is done in anticipation of the change to minimize fluctuations . Examples of feedforward regulation include : • The increased heart rate that occurs in an athlete just before a sprint begins . • The smell of food triggers the secretion of salivary and gastric juices . • An increase in insulin before glucose absorption has raised blood glucose levels .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Positive feedback is seen in all except _____
mcqs.explanation: Positive feedback is seen in all except gastric secretion . It is under negative feedback control. Negative feedback consists of certain changes that affect a deficient or excessive variable to pull it back to a certain mean value to maintain homeostasis . Most processes in the body are under negative feedback . For example , an increase in gastric acids leading to a decrease in gastric secretion . Positive feedback consists of changes that affect a variable to push it further away from a certain mean value. For example , an increase in LH leading to a further increase in LH . Instances, where positive feedback plays an important role are: • Clotting of blood • Calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum • LH Surge • Action potential • Shock • Parturition

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: On infusion of a large volume of blood, the MAP rises from 100 mmHg to 175 mmHg. Due to the baroreceptor feedback mechanism, the MAP falls down to 125 mmHg. Calculate the gain of the feedback system .
mcqs.explanation: The gain of the feedback system in the above case is -2. The gain of the system is then calculated by using the following formula: Gain = C/E Here, C is correction achieved from the deviated value and E is the remaining error post-correction. Calculation12 • The original value in the given case is 100 mmHg. • The deviated value in the given case is 175 mmHg. • The corrected value in the given case is 125 mmHg. • C is given by correction achieved from deviated value, Corrected value - Deviated value = 125 - = -50 mmHg. • E is given by the remaining error post-correction, Corrected value - Original value = 125 - 100 = 25 mmHg. • Gain = -50/25 = -2. The negative symbol indicates that the homeostatic mechanism acts in a direction opposite to the initial deviation.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Plasma membrane in eukaryotes is made up of all except _______
mcqs.explanation: Plasma membrane in eukaryotes does not contain triglycerides . The plasma membrane is composed almost entirely of proteins and lipids . The major lipids include : • Phospholipids : Lecithin, cephalin , phosphatidylserine • Sphingolipids : Sphingomyelin • Cholesterol

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Membrane fluidity is increased by ____.
mcqs.explanation: Membrane fluidity is increased by linoleic acid, an unsaturated fatty acid. All other options are saturated fatty acids. Longer and saturated fatty acids decrease the fluidity because their side chains are straight and interact more strongly with each other. Conversely, unsaturated fatty acids increase the fluidity because their side chains are kinked and less compact. Cholesterol , also known as fluidity buffer helps to maintain the fluidity of the cell membrane.

mcqs.question: The sequence of vesicular transport in a cell is
mcqs.explanation: The sequence of vesicular transport in a cell is ER - Cis - Trans - Cell membrane. Rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER) - It is the site of protein synthesis . mcqs.question: Which of the following will test negative for all mitochondrial markers ?
mcqs.explanation: Mature red blood cells will test negative for all mitochondrial markers are as they do not have mitochondria. Lack of mitochondria is the reason why red blood cells exclusively use anaerobic glycolysis to generate ATP .
